entries.title: Trump Says Iran War May Have Hurt Republicans in the Midterms
entries.summary: The president said he still would have started the war to keep Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
entries.content:
In his first sit-down TV interview since the midterms, President Donald Trump said the Iran war may have hurt Republicans’ chances in the midterms even as he argued the conflict was necessary and was “right for our country.”

“I think historically this will be a very good decision,” Trump told CBS’s “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat. “Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”

Vice President JD Vance appeared to break with Trump in a post to X on Wednesday citing the Iran war as one of the main factors contributing to Republicans’ major losses on Election Day. Trump said he does not “disagree” with Vance’s analysis, but added that he would have launched the war against Iran all over again to prevent the country from having a nuclear weapon.

Some 74% of voters surveyed said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, according to NBC News’ exit polling. With the conflict continuing and fuel prices soaring, the economy remained a top issue for voters in polling ahead of the midterms.

Trump appeared to brush off concerns about high prices and an economic downturn in the “60 Minutes” interview, saying the economic “numbers are phenomenal,” but he acknowledged that Republican losses may have been caused by “bad messaging, maybe by me.”

The prerecorded interview, released Sunday, touched on a wide array of topics including the midterms, Trump’s own net worth, the Russia-Ukraine war, AI and even UFOs. Most notably, Trump said that his deportation policy may have been “too tough,” when asked directly by Douthat about the administration’s approach.

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump said — though he said he believed the immigration crackdown both “helped and hurt” Republicans in the midterms.

Trump also said he would “love to do something on immigration” with Democrats, who will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress come January, and said he has already received calls from Democrats wanting to work on the issue.

“The deal would be we would work something out. I think that's something that's actually doable,” Trump said. “When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as a you know as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great job, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country. It's tough. It's a tough thing.”

NBC News’ exit polling found that 57% of voters believe that the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far — though 22% of the surveyed group also believed the efforts had not gone far enough.

The White House’s “Secure the Border” website touts deporting more than 2.5 million undocumented immigrants since Trump returned to office. That number contains a mix of 605,000 individuals the administration says it deported and 1.9 million people the White House says opted to self-deport, often in fear of facing federal detention pending their removal from the country.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Wage Against the Machine
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 9, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

 In today’s newsletter: D.C.’s minimum wage, dangerous residential construction and a playoff win for the Spirit. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. Sunshine and highs in the 60s are nice, but wind gusts over 30 mph? Not so much. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

With a foie gras ban behind them, D.C. voters will now have to turn their attention to another issue that could hit the ballot as soon as the spring: whether the city should increase its minimum wage to $25 an hour.

A New York-based advocacy group tells The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle that later this week it plans to submit 40,000 signatures to the city’s elections board to get Initiative 87 on the ballot for a special election that’s expected to happen by March or April of next year.

The marquee question that Initiative 87 asks D.C. voters revolves around hiking the minimum wage to $25 by 2029; it’s currently $18.40 an hour. But it also seeks to increase the lower tipped wage — currently $10.30 — that’s paid to bar and restaurant servers so that it meets the prevailing minimum wage.

“The price of everything has gone up,” said Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, which has been coordinating a push for a $25 minimum wage in cities and states across the country. “People are fucking angry about the cost of living in America.”

If the tipped wage question seems like déjà vu, you’re not crazy: D.C. residents voted to phase it out in ballot initiatives in 2018 and 2022, but both were either fully or partially repealed by the D.C. Council.

“My concern lies in the fact we need to be clear-eyed about what this proposal is going to be asking employers to absorb, what it means for workers’ hours and how it impacts hiring, and how much of this cost will be passed down to customers,” says Shawn Townsend, CEO of the Restaurant Association of Metropolitan Washington.

That concern is partially shared by Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George. She tells The Sun that she doesn’t want to move to a $25 minimum wage too quickly, though she still favors phasing out the tipped wage. But, she adds: “We need a strategy that will make D.C. a better place to work and a better place to start a business.”





DEEP DIVE

D.C. residents have complained for years that the city doesn’t do enough to crack down on dangerousresidential construction projects that damage their properties, leave them on the hook for damage and can even lead to buildingcollapses that, in one case,killed a construction worker.

An audit of the Department of Buildings released late last month bore those concerns out, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. It found that DOB has failed to adequately audit the third-party inspectors it contracts with, doesn’t always notify neighbors of adjoining construction projects and doesn’t always collect the required paperwork before issuing permits.

DOB agreed to implement most of the audit’s recommendations, but did call out the selective sampling of the audit — it only looked at eight properties (one from each ward) drawn from a list of 57 that ANCs around D.C. flagged as being possible examples of dangerous construction.

Now that the audit is in, D.C. homeowners want to see council action to enforce changes, particularly as the District looks to ramp up its housing production. DOB issued 63,675 permits in fiscal year 2025, up 23% since fiscal year 2023. That figure will only grow, as Lewis George has ambitious plans to build 72,000 new homes in the next five years.





FROM THE DISTRICT



Standing down: At-large council member Christina Henderson has called off her bid to switch her affiliation from Independent to Democrat and occupy Robert White’s vacated seat, Martin reports.

What ended the weeklong, in-the-weeds saga? Council Chair Phil Mendelson announced that today he will swear in D.C. Democratic Party pick Jamal Holtz, the president of the D.C. Young Democrats, to fill White’s seat and serve as an interim at-large council member instead. D.C. Dems said Holtz will only serve until the party can organize a more open process to select an interim replacement for White, who was elected D.C. Delegate last week.

Several D.C. monuments have gone dark while awaiting repairs from an understaffed and underfunded National Park Service, The Washington Post reports.

A federal judge blocked construction on President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch last week, about two hours after the National Capital Planning Commission voted 8-4 in favor of the 250-foot structure despite enormous public opposition,The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Amazon isn’t done with Loudoun County just yet. The company is planning another data center on 23 acres it purchased last month in Chantilly for almost $100 million, The Washington Business Journal reports.





FROM MARYLAND

With their party set to control congress, Maryland Democrats plan to press the FBI to build its new headquarters in Greenbelt, The Washington Business Journal reports.





TRIVIA


In 1991, D.C. voters shot down a ballot initiative promoted by animal rights activists. What would it have done?

  1. Banned horse-drawn carriages from public streets
  2. Banned animal circus acts from performing in the District
  3. Banned the use of mounted police horses
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Spirit 4, Thorns 1. The Spirit is headed to the NWSL semifinals after an offensive explosion at Audi Field on Sunday afternoon against Portland. With four goals, Washington delivered its best offensive output since early May. Trinity Rodman led the way, scoring twice to continue her fine form. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri has the story from a momentous quarterfinal win.

Washington will host the Utah Royals next weekend at Audi Field.

Rams 20, Commanders 13. Washington falls 2-5-1 after an inconsistent afternoon in Landover. After a strong first half, the Commanders watched their lead — and a prime opportunity for an upset win — slip away after the break. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down Washington’s glaring issues in the defeat, while Dave Sheinin takes a look at how Rams star Puka Nacua (14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown) methodically — and predictably — took over the game.

Trae Young is one of the best players in Atlanta Hawks history. Now, he’s a Wizard. On Friday, Young played against his former team for the first time since they shipped him off to Washington in a salary dump trade. The Sun’s Dave Sheinin went down to Atlanta to write about a complicated homecoming.

What to Watch Today

NBA: Wizards at Pistons, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NFL: Bills at Vikings, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.
entries.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman

entries.title: The Spirit Will Get to Host Their Playoff Game at Audi Field After All
entries.summary: A scheduling conflict was set to require the Spirit to host Saturday’s semifinal with Utah at Washington’s NFL stadium, but the team was able to work out a solution.
entries.content:
Following a statement NWSL quarterfinals win for the Spirit at Audi Field, the details of the next playoff game came booming over the loudspeaker. Washington announced the date, time and opponent, encouraging fans to come out next Saturday at noon to watch the No. 3 seed Spirit host the No. 7 Royals.

Conspicuously absent was the location.

For much of the weekend, it seemed likely that if the Spirit advanced to the semifinals, the club would not be able to host at its usual home of Audi Field. The stadium was booked with a different event for Nov. 14: The Division III football rivalry known as the Secretaries’ Cup, between the Coast Guard Academy and Merchant Marine Academy, which has been scheduled for Audi Field since early August. The alternate location for the Spirit was reported to be Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland, home of the NFL’s Commanders.

This meant that fans left Audi Field on Sunday believing they would be going somewhere else for the semifinals. Players fielded questions in the mixed zone about the potential of spending next weekend in Landover. More than four hours after the match ended, however, the club released some news. The Spirit would be hosting next week at Audi Field, after all.

In a statement, Spirit CEO Kim Stone thanked “the collaboration of D.C. United and the generosity of Lafayette Federal Credit Union, who stepped forward to underwrite the additional costs necessary to bring this semifinal match home.” D.C. United operates Audi Field. The Spirit have been full-time tenants of the stadium since 2023.

The club has built a strong fan environment in the building over those last few years. For Spirit matches, this is “Rowdy Audi,” among the most consistently packed (and consistently loud) stadiums in the NWSL. Washington averaged 16,338 fans for home matches in 2026.

“No matter where we play, we know D.C. will come out and support us,” Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver said after the match, before the club announced the venue. “We want it to be at Audi. But some things are out of our control.”

A semifinal at Northwest Stadium might have brought an opportunity for an unusually large crowd. (The building has a capacity of 64,000, compared to just over 19,000 for Spirit games at Audi Field.) It also would have meant playing on a field that is not designed for soccer in a place the club has never hosted a match before. For players, staff and fans alike, Audi Field is home.

Thirteen-year-old Juniper Ho has followed the team since she was 8. She roots for Trinity Rodman, and when she smiles, her braces flash pink, matching her cherry blossom scarf and her fuchsia “Rowdy” baseball cap, a team giveaway designed by Rodman herself as a nod to Audi Field.

During the quarterfinal match, when many fans believed they would not be returning next week to Audi FIeld, Ho told The Washington Sun that it was “unfortunate” the team could have to relocate.

“It’s a playoff game, so I feel like they should be able to play in their stadium,” said Ho, who attended Sunday’s game with her father.

Some fans drew on a larger frustration with the management of women’s sports. The Spirit was not the only NWSL team faced with getting bumped from its home field during these playoffs. And the WNBA was recently consumed with scheduling conflicts and stadium drama in a saga that saw Game 6 of the WNBA Finals played at 12:30 p.m. on a weekday.

“It just feels like women’s sports are pushed to the backburner,” said Maui Smith, who is a Mystics fan but has recently gotten into the Spirit because she wants to support all local women’s teams. “There’s a lot of good energy at Audi Field. We felt it last week and we certainly feel it now in the playoffs.”

Rodman said the players would have been ready to compete at Northwest Stadium. “At the end of the day, as an athlete, you have to take what you get,” she said in her postgame news conference. “If we do have to play on a different field, that’s what we have to adapt to.” She also said the playoff energy is special in the home environment of Audi Field.

“You feel it from the first whistle, just how loud the stadium is,” she said. “There’s just more passion, obviously from the fans, but from us as well.”

This is the third consecutive trip to the NWSL semifinals for the Spirit.

In recent months, D.C. lawmakers have considered putting $300 million in taxpayer dollars towards a renovation at Audi Field. D.C. United has pledged an additional $320 million to the plan that would add seating and a roof to the stadium, as well as housing on a nearby parcel of land.

D.C. United has argued that the renovation will be necessary when MLS moves to a winter-heavy schedule starting in 2028, and said that the improvements will make the stadium a more in-demand destination for events like concerts. But some Spirit fans believe the negotiations should be an opportunity to ensure the women’s team becomes more integrated in the stadium.

“If the D.C. government is going to give Audi Field money to refurbish, there should be protections in place for D.C.-based teams to have priority,” Kevin Minoli, a Spirit season ticket holder, told The Washington Sun.

The Sun previously reported that the Spirit have discussed upgrades, such as their own locker room and the assurance that the team’s schedule won’t be the first to take a hit when construction is underway, in the renovation discussions.

entries.title: Massie Says Hegseth’s Impeachment Odds Are Up After GOP Midterm Losses
entries.summary: The Republican lawmaker said voting to impeach is “the most practical way” for members to put daylight between themselves and the Iran war.
entries.content:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) said Monday that the chances of the House voting to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are better following the Republicans’ sweeping midterm losses.

“I think the odds went up because of the election,” Massie told The Washington Sun. “There might be some members of Congress who want to put some daylight between themselves and the administration and this war, and this might be the most practical way.”

But he said he hasn’t spoken “to Republicans directly who are committed to supporting it.”

Massie said he expects to renew his impeachment effort on the House floor Monday afternoon after coordinating with House Republican leadership. The House could vote on the resolution as early as Monday night or later this week, he said.

Under the procedure for privileged resolutions, House leaders must take up the matter within two legislative days, Massie said. Opponents could move to table the resolution, which is not debatable, or refer it to committee instead of voting directly on impeachment.

If the resolution survives both actions, or if leaders skip them, the House would vote on the articles of impeachment as soon as Monday.

“The ball is in their court once I give notice,” Massie said of House GOP leaders, “so they have two legislative days. They could deal with it tonight, tomorrow or the next day.”

The effort has gained momentum with House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who announced his support Sunday. Several Republicans have expressed reservations about the defense secretary’s leadership even as President Donald Trump is publicly standing by him.

“I’ve seen some of my colleagues say @SecWar Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach,” Massie said Monday in a post. “That’s not the question though. The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times.”

Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment in September, accusing Hegseth of constitutional violations and abuses of power, including prosecuting the Iran war without congressional authorization and conducting unlawful strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels.

The House never voted on the resolution after Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the remaining floor votes before the midterm recess.

Massie told The Sun he must restart the process because his September notice expired during pro forma sessions. He described the updated articles as “99.99% the same” with minor corrections.

The effort got a big boost Sunday when Jeffries announced his support.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.”

“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” he said. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Jeffries predicted strong support among House Democrats but said lawmakers would discuss the resolution when they meet Tuesday.

Some Republicans have also expressed concerns about Hegseth’s leadership, though few have publicly committed to supporting impeachment.

Rep. French Hill (R-Arkansas), chair of the House Financial Services Committee, on Sunday did not rule out supporting it.

“I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he’s not getting the job done in leading the Department of War,” Hill said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”

Hill said he was dissatisfied with the handling of the Iran war but said it would be up to the president to fire Hegseth.

“If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense,” Hill said. “He's an executive officer of the executive branch, and if he's not conducting his mission in the right way, then the president ought to make a change there.”

Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky) also raised concerns about Hegseth on Friday, telling NewsNation that Republicans were questioning the Pentagon’s handling of the war.

“We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran,” Comer said. “I think Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

Massie called Comer’s remarks “significant” Monday, given the lawmaker’s role as chair of the House Oversight Committee.

Trump, however, has publicly stood by Hegseth, even as news reports suggest the president has privately explored replacing him. CBS News reported that Trump has asked advisers whether Hegseth should stay in the job and that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis had been floated as a possible replacement.

"Look, we've won two wars. We've won Venezuela and taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already," Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview. He added, "And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And, you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want."

Hegseth has been publicly defending himself, releasing a video Thursday in which he accused Massie and Democrats of pursuing political revenge.

“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Whether Hegseth survives the impeachment bid this week, Democrats have vowed extensive congressional investigations when they take control of Congress in January — and if Hegseth remains in the job, a Democrat-led impeachment effort is likely.

Washington Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, has said he would revive an oversight and investigations subcommittee if chosen to chair the full committee.

“Hegseth has ruled the Pentagon in an unbelievably arrogant way,” Smith said Friday on CNN’s “The Arena.” “He has really angered a lot of people — both Republicans and Democrats.”
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: Supreme Court Allows Big Bend Border Wall Construction
entries.summary: The justices lifted a lower-court ruling that had blocked construction along the Big Bend sector in part because of environmental protection laws.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for construction of the Trump administration’s border wall along the Big Bend sector of the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas.

The unsigned decision reverses a lower-court ruling that had ordered the Department of Homeland Security to follow the slew of historical and environmental protection laws that the department had waived this year throughout the region.

The Supreme Court ruling says the lower court’s injunction, which halted all associated construction, overstepped the judge’s legal authority. The high court also said the injunction "impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.”

And the justices said the government’s aims outweigh “any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only noted dissent.

At issue is Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s waivers of over a dozen environmental and historic preservation laws in order to expedite construction in the Big Bend sector, which includes a 607-mile stretch of land at the border, including through state and national parks.

In October, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone denied DHS’s appeal to reverse her earlier ruling.

The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court in an emergency application that called Cardone’s ruling “baseless.” In an October filing, the Trump administration said the district court ruling “understated the harms” that the government would face if construction were not allowed to continue with the laws waived.

The government wrote that the construction is aimed at mitigating border crossings in the Big Bend sector. Lower courts and the plaintiffs say the sector experiences some of the lowest crossing rates across any U.S. border, and the lowest ones along the entire Southern border.

Big Bend-area advocates, including the river boat guide, church preservation and environmental organization that brought the lawsuit against the government, have also said construction in the region would harm local livelihoods that depend on the natural landscape to survive.

The waivers, they wrote in an October filing to the Supreme Court, mark “a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.”

“Once habitat is destroyed, vegetation cleared, historic resources damaged, livelihoods and private property destroyed, and wilderness landscapes fragmented by roads, barriers, and associated infrastructure, no final judgment can restore the status quo,” the group opposing the construction said in a filing.

“The Waivers authorize construction across hundreds of miles of landscape rich with cultural, historical, and archaeological resources that cannot be restored once destroyed,” the filing says.

The government, in its Friday response, called the waivers, “merely a recent example of the Secretary using a well-worn tool in his border-security toolkit.”

The Trump administration campaigned on building a wall against the Southern border, and has awarded billions of dollars in contracts to do so. But that is not without opposition, especially in the Big Bend sector, where the outcry against construction has often been bipartisan, particularly relating to the administration’s efforts in Big Bend National Park and a nearby state park.

This year, Customs and Border Patrol Commissioner Rodney Scott visited the parks following widespread concern over the construction taking place in the area. While there, he announced a voluntary temporary pause in the agency’s plans. The pause expired Sept. 30.
